extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor practitioners, HR/compliance officers, and regulators assessing worker classification under the FLSA
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory criteria and interpretive guidance for determining whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA, using the economic reality totality-of-the-circumstances test and enumerated factors (control, integral, skill & initiative, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to Work for Others (control factor §795.105(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the potential employer limits the worker's ability to work for others, including indirect means of limitation. The final rule revises regulatory language to remove the word “time” and add “or restrictions” after “or places demands” to encompass indirect restrictions such as financial penalties or other constraints that effectively preclude working for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine facts on the ground (e.g., demands on time, monetary penalties, coercive platform practices like threatening termination or reducing work availability unless the worker continuously accepts jobs, prohibitions on developing own customers, being expected to be on call all day). The ability to work for others is one consideration within the control factor; it is relevant but not determinative. The control factor itself is not dispositive—the economic reality test considers the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and Degree of Control (part of control factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which the employer directs or supervises how, when, and where the work is performed, including scheduling, assignment of work locations, direct supervision, and employer policies limiting outside work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete workplace facts and examples: e.g., Alpha House nurses—employer sets schedules, determines work locations, prohibits working for other nursing homes → indicates employee status; Beta House specialist—sets own schedule and price, markets services, not supervised → indicates independent contractor status. Consider both formal policies (e.g., prohibitions on other work) and day-to-day supervision/management practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to Which the Work Performed Is an Integral Part of the Potential Employer's Business (§795.110(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether the work performed is critical, necessary, or central to the employer's principal business (i.e., whether the employer could not function without the service). The factor focuses on the work performed, not whether any particular individual worker is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a common-sense inquiry focused on the employer's principal business—only work that is critical/necessary/central to that principal business is ‘integral.’ Examples: tomato pickers (integral to a farm selling tomatoes) indicate employee status; an outside accountant providing non-payroll accounting is not integral to a farm's principal business → may indicate independent contractor status. Indicators of integration into production processes (e.g., required to work at employer's main workplace, wear employer's uniform) may be relevant and considered under this or other factors. This factor is one part of the totality-of-the-circumstances and is not dispositive; it is distinct from the 2021 Rule's “integrated unit of production” phrasing, and the Department will not treat it as equivalent to the dispositive Prong B of an ABC test. Industry-specific regulatory mandates may inform facts but do not create categorical exemptions; compliance obligations are discussed elsewhere (control factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and Initiative (§795.110(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether the worker uses specialized skills to perform the work and whether those skills are used in connection with business-like initiative. Lack of specialized skills or dependence on employer training tends to indicate employee status; use of specialized skills combined with business-like initiative tends to indicate independent contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reintegrates ‘initiative’ into the skill factor (it had been excluded in the 2021 IC Rule). Evaluate whether specialized skills are applied with business-like initiative (e.g., marketing, setting prices, maintaining a client base). Initiative-related facts may be relevant under multiple factors as appropriate. Examples and sector notes: many occupations (security guards, janitors, drivers, landscape workers, call center workers) are frequently found to lack specialized skills and thus indicate employee status; truck drivers using driving skills plus business-like initiative may indicate independent-contractor status; nurses who employ nursing skills plus business initiative to grow a practice may be independent contractors. As always, this is one factor among many and not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances and Non-dispositive Nature of Enumerated Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic reality test is a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry: all relevant facts and factors must be considered together to determine whether a worker is economically dependent on the potential employer or in business for themself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single enumerated factor is dispositive. This principle differentiates the Department's multifactor economic reality approach from an ABC test (where prongs are dispositive); although conceptual overlap may exist (e.g., integrality and Prong B), the Department's rule treats each factor as one piece of the overall analysis. Courts and agencies may consider additional factors or treat some indicia as supplemental where relevant (e.g., aspects of an 'integrated unit of production' may be relevant under any factor).
